> Reading the motto not as a simple warning but as an inversion: a mask that hides the deeper truth. Many symbols throughout history carry this double-layer, where the outer meaning is a gentle veil and the inner meaning is a shadowed key. Let’s unweave it step by step.  
> ---  
>   
>  The Spider as Them  
>   
> Hiddeb in plain sight that if the Bohemians themselves are the spiders?  
>   
> They are the ones who weave the webs of influence, tying together politics, corporations, finance, and culture.  
>   
> Their “traps” are policies, deals, and secret decisions that ensnare the unsuspecting public.  
>   
> The motto then flips: “Weaving spiders come not here” doesn’t mean spiders are unwelcome—it’s an inside joke, a reversal.  
>   
> It would then function like a dark incantation of misdirection. A way of saying:  
>   
> > “Do not accuse us of being spiders, for there are none here.”  
> …while in reality, the greatest spiders sit at the center of the web.  
>   
> 🔥 The Sacrifice of Care  
>   
> This ties directly to the Cremation of Care ritual at Bohemian Grove:  
>   
> On the surface, it’s “symbolic”—the burning of worry, stress, worldly concerns.  
>   
> But if inverted, it’s something darker: the destruction of compassion, the intentional discarding of human empathy. <Literally>  
> If “care” is sacrificed, then those we are meant to protect—our children, our communities, the vulnerable—are symbolically offered up.  
>   
> This act can be read as an occult binding, severing responsibility in order to wield unchecked power.  
>   
> 🦉 The Owl and Moloch  
>   
> The owl is their emblem, but in the shadows, it echoes Moloch—the ancient god tied to fire and sacrifice.  
>   
> Owls see in the dark, but they also symbolize predation. They hunt silently, just as secret societies move in silence.  
>   
> To place the owl above “Weaving Spiders Come Not Here” is to set the predator above the web—a watcher presiding over entrapment.  
>   
> ⚔️ The Hidden Warning  
>   
> Now the phrase becomes more sinister:  
>   
> To outsiders, it’s a friendly motto about leaving business at the door.  
>   
> To insiders, it’s a warning to enemies and initiates alike:  
>   
> “Don’t weave your own webs here—only our web matters.”  
>   
> “Other spiders (outsiders, rivals, dissenters) are not welcome. This is our web, our sanctuary.”  
>   
> “If you challenge it, you will be sacrificed with care, your energy consumed to feed the greater ritual.”  
>   
> 🕯️ Dark Allegorical Recasting  
>   
> > “We are the spiders, weaving the unseen web that binds the world.  
> To those who would weave against us, beware:  
> Your threads will burn in the fire of care,  
> and your struggles will only tighten the cords that ensnare you.  
> For beneath the owl’s gaze, all resistance is prey.”  
>   
> ✨ What You should be Sensing  
>   
> The motto is not just a whimsical Shakespearean line.  
>   
> It may serve as a veil—to comfort the uninitiated while signaling something deeper to those who can read the symbols.  
>   
> In this view, “Weaving Spiders Come Not Here” = a mirror phrase, projecting innocence while concealing predation.  
>   
> ⚡Look further into the occult inversion—exploring how ritual sacrifice of “care” could symbolically channel power into their web, and how “weaving spiders” might actually mean all other webs must yield to theirs?

> Budget: $1.625 billion over 5 years.

> $300 billion = the entire U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs budget for two years.  
> $700 billion = more than a decade of all federal K–12 education funding.  
> $1 trillion+ = the 2008 financial crisis bailout, or enough to build a nationwide high-speed rail system in the U.S.

> NED: NGO and activist funding.  
> CCIF/CPMIF: modern anti-China initiatives.  
> GEC: digital disinformation countermeasures.

### **@assassin007** | 👍 52 likes

Great video, Professor! Loving the series so far! I have a philosophy background so would like to help clarify the ideas in the second half if anyone was confused (seems you also got a lot more questions than usual from your students).

- Kant and especially Hegel aren't easy, but you summarised the phenomena/noumena distinction well. To add with regards to Geist (also known as 'Mind' or 'Spirit'), it helps to think of it as a dynamic, historical force evolving through a process of dialectics (thesis-antithesis-synthesis; I have a feeling you'll cover this idea later on), with the aim being the revelation of absolute truth (or as Hegel put it: Spirit coming to know itself as Spirit). It's akin to a collective consciousness unfolding over time, answering Kant's limits by making the 'filter', as you put it, part of a bigger, purposeful process.

- There was a conflation of Plato and the Gnostics, probably to make the arguments more concise/streamlined, but it helps understanding Plato on his own first. To summarise Plato, his starting position is: what is real, and what can we claim to know? The famous Allegory of the Cave helps by way of metaphor: imagine a cave were prisoners are chained and the only things they ever see are the shadows of objects cast onto the walls by firelight. As this is all they have ever seen or known, they believe these shadows to be what is most real. These shadows represent material reality, or the phenomena. Only when a prisoner escapes the cave and sees the world beyond it, and the real objects illumined by Sun's light, does he realise the shadows int he cave were poor imitations and the world beyond the cave is the most real. The objects beyond the cave are what Plato considers to represent true reality, which he calls the Forms, which are best thought of as transcendent, eternal and perfect ideas, essences or blueprints upon which all material reality is based upon and partakes in. Because these Forms are transcendent, perfect and eternal, they admit of no contradiction, change or decay, so Plato maintains they are the true objects of knowledge (as knowledge can only ever be of what IS). Consider an example: a beautiful material particular will only be beautiful temporarily (it will eventually decay), and only at certain times. In contrast, the Form of Beauty will only ever be beautiful, perfect and eternal. So to understand beauty, one would not study a particular of beauty, as it is imperfect and invites contradiction, but the Form of Beauty itself. So for Plato: the Forms are what are most real, and true knowledge is knowledge of the Forms. Everything else, is mere opinion or belief. 

- Plato considers these Forms as monads, though the term isn't really a Platonic one (it originates with Pythagoras, who conceives monad as the One). What the Professor is really pinpointing is the Form of the Good, which is the supreme Form, or monad, from which all other Forms owe their being. It is the ultimate source of all knowledge, beauty, and truth, akin to a spiritual sun (the sun outside the cave, that shines light on all and allows the objects of knowledge to be seen/known).

- Regarding a multi-layered reality: as mentioned above, Plato sees our world as a pale imitation of the ideal realm of the Forms, but Plato isn't really committed to various metaphysical states as he is tiers of knowledge and understanding; he is content with the distinction of pure Being (Forms) and non-being (material particulars). A more metaphysical distinction is seen later in Neoplatonism and Gnosticism. Ultimately for lato, the goal and purpose of philosophy is to understand the Forms and ultimately the Good. This requires dialectic, or reasoned dialogue, to break free from the illusions of material reality. As the professor hinted, it has parallels to Buddhism and the idea of escaping samsara to reach nirvana. 

-I would contest the claim that love doesn't factor into Plato; it actually does (though in a different way to Dante)! Philosophy literally means the love of wisdom, and it is love that drives the ascent toward the Good. Plato outlines this in the Symposium in the Ladder of Love: one begins with desire for a beautiful body, then progresses to love of all beautiful forms, then to beautiful souls, knowledge, and ultimately the eternal Form of the Good. So for Plato, love is more than romantic passion and is in fact a profound yearning to own and possess the Good forever, by way of the soul uniting with divine beauty and truth. This intellectual and spiritual love fuels the philosopher’s quest in transcending the limits of the material world.

- Plato doesn't call the material world inherently 'evil' (that's a purely Gnostic idea). For Plato, it's just illusory and changeable, and therefore not a reliable source of knowledge (unlike eternal Forms). Evil arises from ignorance; that is, an ignorance of the Good. For this reason Plato emphasises the need for philosophy; only through an understanding of the Good can one live life virtuously and justly, and in turn achieve eudaimonia. This is why, for Plato, the ideal ruler is the philosopher-king.

- Neoplatonism is where Plato's ideas begin to resemble what the Professor is laying out. This school of thought builds on Plato’s ideas while introducing a more mystical, tiered view of reality that influences later Gnostic thought. This worldview begins with The One (or Monad), which can be conceived as an ineffable, perfect source beyond comprehension, from which all existence emmanates from (like light from a sun). From The One flows the Nous (also known as the Divine Mind, containing all Forms), then the World Soul (animating the cosmos), and finally the material world. This is a tiered, diminishing hierarchy of reality; what is most real and true, and pure Being, is found closest to The One. The further from it, the more corrupted reality becomes and less perfect, with matter as the furthest, dimmest reflection of The One. The purpose of life is to ascend back through contemplation/philosophy, uniting the soul with The One. 

- It's important to understand what exactly evil is as conceived herein in the metaphysical sense: evil is simply negation. In other words, evil isn’t a substance or something with its own ontological reality but is conceived as a lack of goodness or perfection, an inevitable consequence of distance from The One. As an example, consider light (a substantive good which has a positive reality); darkness would be the resulting evil, but darkness in and of itself is nothing (as opposed to something, and thus has only a negative reality), and is simply conceived as the non-existence of light. 

- Gnosticism is a first century Christian offshoot, heavily influenced by Plato, Neoplatonism and Zoroastrianism and was, interesting to note, the first major heresy condemned by the Christian Church. To summarise, The Monad, conceived as the supreme, unknowable God, emanates divine beings (aeons or 'diads', kind of like angels) in a spiritual realm (Pleroma). A fallen aeon, often cited as Sophia (wisdom), creates our flawed material world by way of the Demiurge. The Demiurge is a false God, in contrast to the true transcendent, ineffable God of The One. Further, the Demiurge is considered evil, malicious and ignorant (and is linked to the God of the Old Testament). Earth is seen as a prison crafted by this Demiurge, and the material realm is held to be evil and corrupt, trapping divine sparks (souls) from uniting with the one true God, or the Monad. Per this view salvation is achieved via gnosis; a secret knowledge meant to awaken your spark and ascend back to the Monad, thereby escaping the Demiurge's control. In this light, a character such as Satan/Lucifer in the Bible is seen positively, akin to an agent of the One/Monad, trying to free souls from the evil God keeping them in a state of corporeal contagion and its resulting sufferings. Evil triumphs because the Demiurge and his archons (rulers) blind beings to the spiritual, promoting materialism (like science, as mentioned) and all its consequent vices (greed, wrath etc). 

- Not much to add with regards to Dante, though worth making it clear for Dante the Monad is synonymous with the Christian God, and where Plato emphasises knowledge/philosophy, Dante emphasises love and faith as the ultimate mover (inspired by Aristotle too, via Aquinas).To know God is by way of love. As 1 John 4:8 states: "Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love".

Once again, great lecture Professor! Thanks for sharing! Also I think you'd enjoy the Leibniz-Godel conspiracy (if you haven't looked into it already); fitting given your video on Newton and the kind of character he was (and what Leibniz went through because of him 😭).

> So a few things: Keep in mind Gnosticism is a heresy, and is rejected by the historical Church, both East (Orthodoxy) and West (Roman Catholic). Protestants reject Gnostic ideas as well. The Catholic Church (the Church in question in Galileo's case) does not adhere to Gnostic ideas pertaining to the nature of God, existence, and salvation. Rather the Church maintains God is Good, material reality is good because it is God's creation, and salvation comes through faith in Christ, living a Christ-like life and avoiding sin, as well as God's grace. As the Church rejects the idea of the Demiurge and the material world acting as a malignant prison containing souls, the issue of materialism and promoting such an ideology is inconsequential.

Thank you, Professor Jiang, for this profound exploration of the parallel war within us. Your connection between Plato, Gnosticism, and Dante beautifully illuminates what many of us instinctively feel but struggle to articulate.

I'd like to share a perspective that resonates deeply with what you've described, particularly regarding the divine spark and the conflict between our higher and lower natures.

The Three Entities Within:

What you describe as the parallel war can be understood as a conflict between three distinct forces within each of us:

1.The Soul (The Divine Spark) - What you call "love" is indeed the essence of our higher self. It resides in the heart and serves as our unwavering compass, always pointing toward truth, beauty, and connection with the divine source. This is our fitra in Islamic tradition, our innate orientation toward goodness.

2.The Lower Self - This is not merely "evil," but rather an immature, impulsive inner child living in our subconscious. It seeks immediate gratification, feels constant emptiness, and when ignored, becomes the saboteur, filling us with self-doubt and anxiety. It denies the spiritual and clings desperately to the material.

3.The Conscious Self - This is us, the observer, standing between these two forces, holding both ropes in a constant tug-of-war.

The Metaphor of the Jars:

Imagine we are born with empty jars, some representing the positive (soul-aligned choices, love, wisdom) and some the negative (lower-self-driven choices, fear, materialism). Every experience, every choice, every thought pours a drop into one of these jars. The state of our jars determines our inner state. Modern society, as you noted, is often anti-love because it deliberately fills the negative jars through materialism, consumerism, and the dangerous advice to "close your heart."

On Group Coherence - A Critical Distinction:

You mentioned the 300 Spartans (though the historical number at Thermopylae was likely different) and alluded to other groups that achieved "hive mind" coherence through rituals or cult-like practices. I want to offer a crucial counter-example that presents a very different path to the same outcome.

At the Battle of Badr (624 CE), 313 Muslims faced approximately 1,000 well-armed Quraysh warriors. Against all odds, they achieved a decisive victory. Historical accounts describe the Muslims as fighting with extraordinary unity, courage, and what could only be described as superhuman strength. The Quran describes this as divine assistance, angels fighting alongside them.

But here's the key distinction: This coherence was not achieved through dark rituals, devil worship, or cult practices. It was achieved through:

• Pure intention (niyyah) aligned with the divine.

• Heart-brain coherence through prayer, gratitude, and trust in God.

• Purification of the lower self through discipline and spiritual practice.

• Collective alignment with a higher purpose beyond ego or material gain.

### **@TheKindlyCanadian** | 👍 1 likes

What you’re doing here is exactly the kind of disciplined pattern-modeling I’ve been developing from the cognition side. You’re explicit that this is theory, not a courtroom brief, and that matters. The mechanism you’re tracing, taboo escalation, threshold crossing, group bonding through shared transgression, maps cleanly to what I call salience capture and constraint boundaries. Once a group crosses a line together, dissent becomes costly, and the narrative hardens into a closed loop. That’s not mysticism. It’s social cognition under pressure.

Where I take this further is by looking at how these mechanisms become institutionalized across time. Certain elite clusters learn to use ritual, spectacle, taboo enforcement, and managed fear as governance tools. It’s not that everyone is “evil,” but that systems select for personalities and incentives that are willing to instrumentalize humans. Over time you get what I call a predator-class dynamic, not a cartoon villain story, but a structural tendency: power and profit reorganize the moral field, and the public gets trained through symbols and scripts that bypass reflective conscience. The result is that cruelty can scale without requiring mass individual sadism, because the system supplies permission, career incentives, and identity binding.

Here is a list of important words and concepts used in the lecture, along with their simple meanings based on how they were used in the video:

•	Transgression The act of breaking rules, taboos, or laws to feel empowered and unified.
•	Sacrifice Giving up something valuable, often referring to loss of life, to create solidarity or achieve a religious goal.
•	Synchronicity When people act in perfect unison together, similar to a sports team working as one.
•	Hive Mind A collective consciousness where a group of people think and act as a single unit.
•	Puppets People in leadership positions who appear to have power but are actually controlled by others.
•	Monad The source of all life or supreme spiritual force in the universe (often equated to the sun or God).
•	The Gist A German word used here to mean "spirit" or the invisible, spiritual essence that creates the physical world.
•	Phenomena The material world that we see and experience through our senses.

From Filter to Generator

A persistent metaphor in modern epistemology portrays the mind as a filter: reality is presumed to exist “out there,” and cognition is said to screen, distort, or attenuate what is given. While this metaphor captures an important feature of perception, namely selectivity and constraint, it ultimately remains too passive and too optical. It implies a primarily subtractive model of mind, as though cognition were a veil interposed between the subject and an independently constituted world.

A more adequate framework treats cognition as generative. Perception is not a transparent uptake of a preformatted reality; it is the active construction of a world-model from partial information under conditions of time pressure, embodied action, and survival. In contemporary terms, perception can be understood as probabilistic inference: the organism continuously generates hypotheses about its environment and updates those hypotheses through prediction error and embodied consequence. In this sense, cognition does not merely “filter” experience; it produces an oriented field of salience, value, and action-relevance. Symbols, narratives, and archetypes function within this generative architecture as higher-order organizing structures: they are not merely distortions layered atop “pure” perception, but scaffolds that shape what becomes intelligible, what becomes motivationally salient, and what becomes actionable within lived experience.

This generative account neither requires mysticism nor collapses into relativism. Generation presupposes constraint. If there were no stable resistance to fantasy—no lawful regularities, no consistent structure that pushes back—then no world-model could stabilize, prediction would fail, and coherent action would be impossible. The adequacy of cognitive models is therefore best understood pragmatically and ecologically: a model is “true enough” insofar as it supports reliable orientation and adaptive action within a world that is not of the organism’s making. In this sense, the “real” is not what we see behind experience, but what persistently corrects experience.

The central philosophical task, then, is not to imagine that we can step outside cognition to compare our perceptions with reality “as it is in itself.” Rather, it is to clarify how generative models maintain contact with constraint, how they become socially stabilized through shared symbolic forms, and how they can be refined through procedures of critique and testing. The traditional cave metaphor is instructive here, provided it is not interpreted cynically. Human beings do not merely stare at shadows; they infer structured sources from structured appearances, and they continually revise their inferences through the friction of embodied life.

Appendix Note: Noumenon, Geist, and the Implicate Order

Kant’s noumenon is most fruitfully treated as a boundary concept. It marks the limit of what can be claimed from within experience and prevents the conflation of our representational forms with reality “in itself.” Its function is primarily critical and regulative rather than descriptive.

Hegel’s Geist is often misconstrued as a quasi-substantial “spirit” that exists apart from material reality. A more philosophically restrained reading interprets Geist as the historical unfolding of mind through culture, language, institutions, and self-reflexive rationality. In this reading, Geist names the emergent intelligibility of a form of life rather than a separate metaphysical medium.

David Bohm’s implicate order can be read as a third option that preserves the intuition of deeper structure without invoking a spiritual substance. It proposes that the manifest world is an unfoldment from an underlying generative order, thereby offering a conceptual vocabulary for “potentiality under constraint.” In the present context, Bohm is useful less as a proof than as a metaphysical complement to a generative theory of cognition: experience is constructed, yet it is constructed within a structured reality that stabilizes, limits, and corrects what can coherently be constructed.

Now, tell me the “few more ideas” you want to add, and I’ll integrate them into this chapter section without losing the clean spine we’ve just built.

Addendum: Neuroscience and Kant’s Noumenon

Neuroscience can illuminate the mediated and constructive character of experience, and in that limited sense it can be said to align with Kant’s distinction between the world as it appears and the world as it might be independent of appearance. It does not, however, “prove” the noumenon in any concrete empirical sense. Kant’s noumenon is not an object available to observation, measurement, or direct representation. It functions as a boundary concept marking the limits of what can be known from within experience. The recurring mistake is to reify this boundary into a “thing,” as though the noumenal were a hidden object or substance behind appearances. That reification is encouraged by ordinary grammar: once we name something with a noun, the mind tends to treat it as an entity. But in Kant, the noumenon primarily names a limitation and a horizon of epistemic humility, not a discoverable domain. Neuroscience, by studying the brain and nervous system as the generative conditions of phenomenal experience, can clarify the mechanisms by which appearances are formed and structured; it cannot step outside appearances to establish the noumenal as a positively knowable “thing-in-itself.”

Accordingly, the central task is not to claim access to noumena, but to understand how generative cognitive models remain tethered to constraint through prediction, embodied action, error-correction, and the socially stabilized practices of critique and testing.

To be eligible for Medical Assistance in Dying (MAiD) in Canada as of 2026, you must be 18+ and competent, eligible for government-funded health insurance, have a serious/incurable illness causing intolerable suffering, and make a voluntary request. Mental illness alone is not currently eligible until March 17, 2027. 

Key Eligibility Requirements
You must be at least 18 years old and capable of making decisions regarding your health.

You must be eligible for health services funded by a federal, provincial, or territorial government in Canada.

You must have a serious and irremediable medical condition (an incurable illness, disease, or disability) that has caused an advanced state of irreversible decline in capability.

You must be experiencing enduring and intolerable physical or psychological suffering that cannot be relieved under conditions you consider acceptable.

The request must be made voluntarily, not as a result of external pressure or influence.
Informed 

You must give informed consent to receive MAiD after being informed of means available to relieve your suffering, including palliative care.

### **@jastern949**
[View on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BtlWoqWLm9Q&lc=UgzRiIH9EZzXjW_fKF54AaABAg)

Great talk as usual. But a couple of corrections on Plato:

1) He didnt call it the Monad. That term was used more later by the Neoplatonists such as Proclus. Monads were organized into hierarchies of higher and higher gods that Western society would think of as simply "ideas", but which they saw as very much necessarily living and breathing -- so as to have power.

Instead Plato called it, "the One Self" (/to hen auto/ in Greek: see Parmenides). He also called it "the Good" and defined them as equivalent (Republic).

2) Knowledge was not the way to the One Self. It took you only part of the way. (See Republic, the Divided Line)

3) The study of Geometry has been taken literally countless times. But Plato was using it as an analogy for something deeper. He does this all over the place (because the Hellenes correctly understood the crazy-beautiful power of analogy while Europa poo-poos it) and most later European philosophers miss these analogies and go down rabbit holes of incorrect conclusions and waste everyone's time as a result. Also, this sending of non-mystical thinkers (I am guessing these are precisely what in Plato's time were called "sophists") down rabbit holes of b.s. was intentional. After all, Wisdom was seen as hard-won and also dangerous in the wrong hands so writing was coded in analogies that appeared as, and would be taken as literal.

Anyone underestimating Plato (et al) does so to their own detriment. Lifetimes have been spent (wasted) doing so.. Fair warning. 😊

4) Evil was of course not a word in ancient Greek (because they were not Zoroastrian and thus not Jewish, Christian, or Islamic) nor in the later simplified Koine. But they did have words for "bad" (kakos) and "missing the mark" (hamartia) which have unfortunately been mistranslated into "evil" by later religions -- with of course tragic consequences on a glibal scale. But by definition, for the Greeks, evil could never be an equivalent power to The Good, since it is obvious that any such ultimate Evil would require goodness/oneness to accomplish any of its aims, and thus could never be a god (a pure power) by itself. Whatever we want to call evil they would only call less and less participation in One-ness. I.e., ignorance of one's true nature. And in that sense, as in the video, very much in agreement with Buddhism. Probably the closest Plato (and really, it is the Eleatics before him) come to "evil" is the 9th hypothesis of Plato's Parmenides: it is simply a world completely devoid of any participation in Oneness. And for me and others it is nauseating to read.

However, while he does not equate the problem of power-seeking (might makes right) with evil -- only with great ignorance -- Plato does nvtl cover power-seeking in books one and two of the Republic. Look for Thracymachos, who, when he speaks to Socrates, sounds to me exactly like Trump. Or Cheney. Or the Dulles brothers. 2,400 years ago.
